rationale: A wins because it turns the same facts into cleaner, beat-specific stories and demands the ugly proof before anyone gets cute. Its strongest line is the real story: "Oatly cuts the carbon footprint of its barista oat milk by 31% while closing a US plant." B is useful, but "Oatly launches its lowest-footprint product while closing a US plant" overclaims the evidence; lower than the old formula is not lowest-footprint, and that is how you buy yourself a correction.
gaps_in_A: "A 1,400-store coffee chain makes oat milk the default, not the upcharge" risks implying the chain removed the non-dairy surcharge. The update only says default non-dairy option; A knows this because its own proof asks whether an upcharge exists.

"unprofitable plant-based companies retreat from sustainability spending" is a plausible tension, but the update does not say the reformulation cost more or represented incremental sustainability spending.

"If the LCA report and a named chain contact are not obtainable this week... pitch only the foodservice angle" is muddled. Without a named chain contact, the foodservice angle is the first one that collapses.
gaps_in_B: "Oatly launches its lowest-footprint product" is invented. The fact is 31% lower than the previous formula, not lowest across Oatly's portfolio.
"what it means for upcharges and waste" drags in waste without support. Ask about upcharges, fine; waste needs a supplied operational fact.
"That reporter tests whether this is a category correction or a company-specific turnaround" reaches past the update. One narrowing loss plus one plant closure does not earn a turnaround frame.
"Five viable shapes exist" is inflated because one is explicitly "not a pitch to send." Useful defensive prep, yes; viable press outreach angle, no.
